Nationalism in India

The First World War, the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh made nationalism a mass force. This chapter follows the Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements, the Salt March, the Poona Pact, and the symbols and images through which Indians came to see themselves as one nation.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

As the First World War broke out in 1914, the nationalist movement in India entered a new phase. The war created a new economic and political situation — huge defence expenditure, customs duties raised, income tax introduced, prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, forced recruitment and the influenza epidemic of 1918–19 — and the failure of the British to deliver self-government after the war produced deep anger.

Gandhiji returned to India in January 1915 and introduced satyagraha — the appeal to conscience, the power of truth and non-violence — in Champaran (1916), Kheda (1917) and Ahmedabad (1918). The Rowlatt Act of 1919, which allowed detention without trial, was met with a nationwide hartal; on 13 April 1919 General Dyer fired on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds, and the brutality — including the crawling order — turned nationalism into a mass movement.

The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) combined the Khilafat issue with swaraj and asked people to surrender titles, boycott schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth, with the proposed programme moving to full civil disobedience. It ended abruptly after Chauri Chaura in February 1922. Within the movement, different social groups — middle class, peasants, tribals, plantation workers, women — joined for their own reasons and on their own terms.

The Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Salt March of 12 March–6 April 1930, from Sabarmati to Dandi, and with it the breaking of the salt law. It produced the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, the Second Round Table Conference, the Poona Pact of 1932 and the Communal Award controversy, and revealed the limits of a movement built on non-violence when it faced workers, peasants and dalits with their own demands. The chapter closes with the sense of collective belonging — images of Bharat Mata, the flag, folklore and icons — through which the nation was imagined.

Satyagraha

The idea of appealing to conscience through truth and non-violence; a satyagrahi wins by persuasion, not force, and can succeed only if the cause is just and the opponent is willing to see the truth.

Rowlatt Act (1919)

An Act under which the government could detain political prisoners without trial for two years; it was passed despite opposition by Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council.

Jallianwala Bagh

The enclosed ground in Amritsar where General Dyer fired on a peaceful gathering on 13 April 1919, killing hundreds and wounding many more.

Khilafat Movement

A movement led by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali to defend the Ottoman Khalifa’s spiritual authority, which Gandhiji joined to bring Hindus and Muslims together.

Swaraj

Self-rule; in the Non-Cooperation programme it meant, if necessary, the surrender of titles and boycott of schools, courts, councils and foreign goods.

Awadh Peasant Movement

The movement led by Baba Ramchandra against talukdars and landlords who demanded high rents and illegal cesses.

Poona Pact (1932)

The agreement between Gandhiji and Dr B.R. Ambedkar giving the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, to be voted in by the general electorate.

Civil Disobedience

Breaking colonial laws openly and peacefully — beginning with the salt law in 1930 — and accepting the punishment.

Bharat Mata

The image of India as a mother figure, first painted by Abanindranath Tagore in 1905, which became a symbol of national identity.

Vande Mataram

Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s song in praise of the motherland, included in his novel Anandamath and widely sung during the Swadeshi movement.

The First World War, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation

As the First World War broke out in 1914, the nationalist movement in India entered a new phase. The war created a new economic and political situation: huge defence expenditure led to a price rise and hardship for common people; customs duties were raised and income tax introduced; prices nearly doubled between 1913 and 1918; villagers were forcibly recruited for the army, causing widespread anger; and in 1918–19 and 1920–21 crops failed in many parts of India, resulting in acute food shortages, accompanied by an influenza epidemic in which, according to the 1921 Census, 12 to 13 million people perished.

People hoped that their hardships would end after the war was over. But that did not happen — and at this stage a new leader appeared, and a new mode of struggle.

The idea of satyagraha

Satyagraha

Satyagraha — the idea of appealing to conscience. Gandhiji returned to India in January 1915 and successfully organised satyagraha movements in various places. In 1916 he travelled to Champaran in Bihar to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive plantation system; in 1917 he organised a satyagraha to support the peasants of the Kheda district of Gujarat, affected by crop failure and a plague epidemic, who could not pay the revenue and demanded it be relaxed; and in 1918 he went to Ahmedabad to champion the cause of the cotton mill workers.

The idea of satyagraha emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth. It suggested that if the cause was true, if the struggle was against injustice, then physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor. Without seeking vengeance or being aggressive, a satyagrahi could win the battle through non-violence — by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor, who had to be persuaded to see the truth instead of being forced to accept truth through the use of violence. This could be done by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor. People — including the oppressors — had to be persuaded to see the truth, instead of being forced to accept truth through the use of violence. By this struggle, truth was bound to ultimately triumph.

The Rowlatt Act

Gandhiji in 1919 decided to launch a nationwide satyagraha against the proposed Rowlatt Act (1919). This Act had been hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council despite the united opposition of the Indian members. It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities, and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years.

On 6 April 1919 Gandhiji started a nationwide hartal — “day of opposition to the Rowlatt Act” — with rallies and processions, and strikes in railway workshops and shops. The British administration decided to clamp down on nationalists: local leaders were picked up from Amritsar, Gandhiji was barred from entering Delhi, and on 10 April police in Amritsar fired upon a peaceful procession, provoking widespread attacks on banks, post offices and railway stations. Martial law was imposed and General Dyer took command.

On 13 April 1919 a crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh. Some came to protest against the government’s new repressive measures and others to attend the annual Baisakhi fair. Being from outside the city, many villagers were unaware of the martial law. Dyer entered the area, blocked the exit points and opened fire on the crowd, killing hundreds. His object, as he declared later, was to “produce a moral effect”, to create in the minds of satyagrahis a feeling of terror and awe.

As the news of Jallianwala Bagh spread, crowds took to the streets in many north Indian towns. There were strikes, clashes with the police and attacks on government buildings. The government responded with brutal repression: satyagrahis were forced to rub their noses on the ground, crawl on the streets and do salaam (salute) to all sahibs; people were flogged and villages (around Gujranwala in Punjab, now in Pakistan) were bombed. Seeing violence spread, Gandhiji called off the movement.

Why non-cooperation?

In his famous book Hind Swaraj (1909) Mahatma Gandhi declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians, and had survived only because of this cooperation. If Indians refused to cooperate, British rule in India would collapse within a year, and swaraj would come.

How could non-cooperation become a movement? Gandhiji proposed that the movement should unfold in stages: the surrender of titles that the government awarded, and a boycott of civil services, army, police, courts and legislative councils, schools and foreign goods. Then, in case the government used repression, a full civil disobedience campaign would be launched. Through the summer of 1920 Gandhiji and Shaukat Ali toured extensively, mobilising popular support for the movement.

Many within the Congress were, however, reluctant to boycott the council elections scheduled for November 1920, and they feared that the movement might lead to popular violence. In the months between September 1920 and December 1920 there was an intense tussle within the Congress. At the Congress session at Nagpur in December 1920, a compromise was worked out and the Non-Cooperation programme was adopted.

The Khilafat issue

The First World War had ended with the defeat of Ottoman Turkey, and there were rumours that a harsh peace treaty was going to be imposed on the Ottoman emperor — the spiritual head of the Islamic world (the Khalifa). To defend the Khalifa’s temporal powers, a Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919 under the leadership of Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali. Gandhiji saw this as an opportunity to bring Muslims under the umbrella of a unified national movement: at the Calcutta session of the Congress in September 1920 he convinced other leaders to start a non-cooperation movement in support of Khilafat as well as for swaraj.

The Non-Cooperation Movement and Its Spread

The movement started in January 1921. It was a truly mass movement, with people from all walks of life participating. The colonial government responded with repression: hundreds of students left government-controlled schools and colleges, and many lawyers gave up their practice. The Council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party, the party of the non-Brahmans, felt that entering the council was one way of gaining some power — something that usually only Brahmans had access to.

Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed, and foreign cloth burnt in huge bonfires. The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore. In many places merchants and traders refused to trade in foreign goods or finance foreign trade. As the boycott movement spread, and people began discarding imported clothes and wearing only Indian ones, production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up.

But this movement in the cities gradually slowed down for a variety of reasons. Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth and poor people could not afford to buy it. So the boycott of foreign cloth could not be sustained for long. Similarly the boycott of British institutions posed a problem: for the movement to be successful, alternative Indian institutions had to be set up so that they could be used in place of the British ones. These were slow to come up, and so students and teachers began trickling back to government schools and lawyers joined back work in government courts.

The movement in the countryside

In the countryside the movement was led by peasants and tribals, who joined for their own reasons and with their own demands.

Chauri Chaura and the withdrawal

In February 1922 at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district, a peaceful procession turned into a violent clash and the police station was set on fire, killing 22 policemen. Gandhiji decided to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement — he felt that the movement was turning violent and satyagrahis needed to be properly trained before they could be ready for mass struggles. Within the Congress, some leaders were by now tired of mass struggles and wanted to participate in elections to the provincial councils that had been set up by the Government of India Act of 1919 — and they felt it was important to oppose British policies from within the councils, argue for reform and demonstrate that these councils were not truly democratic. C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics. Younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for more radical mass agitation and for full independence.

Towards Civil Disobedience

In the late 1920s Indian politics was dominated by two different strands. On the one hand was the Simon Commission: in February 1928 a commission arrived in India to look into the working of the constitutional system, headed by Sir John Simon — and since it did not contain a single Indian member, it was greeted with the slogan “Go back Simon” by all parties, and Lala Lajpat Rai led a demonstration at Lahore in which he was beaten by the police and died of his injuries. On the other hand was the demand for “Purna Swaraj”: at the Lahore session of the Congress in December 1929, under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru, the demand for full independence was formalised, and 26 January 1930 was to be observed as Independence Day.

The Salt March

Gandhiji found in salt a powerful symbol of resistance. On 31 January 1930 he sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands, the most stirring of which was the demand to abolish the salt tax, since salt was consumed by the rich and the poor alike and was one of the most essential items of food. The letter was an ultimatum: if the demands were not fulfilled by 11 March, the Congress would launch a civil disobedience campaign.

On 12 March 1930 Gandhiji started his famous march from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 of his trusted volunteers. Walking about 10 miles a day, over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi, the volunteers reached the coast on 6 April 1930 and Gandhiji broke the salt law by manufacturing salt from sea water. As the news of the march spread, foreign cloth was boycotted, liquor shops picketed, peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes, village officials resigned and in many places forest people violated forest laws by going into reserved forests to collect wood and graze cattle.

The government responded with a policy of brutal repression: about 1,00,000 people were arrested, including Abdul Ghaffar Khan, and Gandhiji himself was arrested. A frightened government decided on a policy of repression — and in April 1930 Gandhiji was arrested, followed by the arrest of Abdul Ghaffar Khan. The British had to face the wrath of the people — in Sholapur, crowds attacked police posts, municipal buildings, law courts and railway stations, and in Peshawar in the North-West Frontier Province, a frightened government responded with a policy of brutal repression, and peaceful satyagrahis were attacked, women and children were beaten, and about 1,00,000 people were arrested.

The movement was called off when Gandhiji entered into the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931: the government agreed to release the political prisoners, and Gandhiji agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London and to call off the movement. The Congress had been asked to call off the movement, and the government had agreed to release the political prisoners. In December 1931 Gandhiji went to London for the conference, but the negotiations broke down and he returned disappointed.

The limits and the second phase

In the countryside, rich peasant communities — Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh — were active in the movement. Being producers of commercial crops, they were very hard hit by the trade depression and falling prices. As their cash income disappeared, they found it impossible to pay the government’s revenue demand; the refusal of the government to reduce the revenue led to a militant response, and in many places the government had to be forced to reduce the revenue. But once their demands were met, they became less enthusiastic about a movement that was not concerned with their problems.

Poor peasants had a different grievance: as tenants they had no security of tenure, being regularly evicted so that they could acquire no right over the leased land. The business classes were also unhappy with the movement — they had made huge profits during the First World War and had become powerful; they wanted protection against imports of foreign goods and a rupee-sterling exchange ratio that would discourage imports, and they were worried about the disruption of trade caused by the movement. They gave financial assistance and refused to buy or sell imported goods, but once the movement was called off in 1931 they were disappointed, and when it was relaunched in 1932 many of them did not participate.

The participation of women was large — in towns and cities thousands of women came out of their homes to listen to Gandhiji, to take part in protest marches, manufacture salt and picket foreign cloth and liquor shops. But the Congress was kept away from the dalit community — the Congress had ignored the dalits for fear of offending the sanatanis, the conservative high-caste Hindus — and Gandhiji’s fast to persuade the upper castes to change their hearts did not satisfy Dr B.R. Ambedkar, who demanded separate electorates for dalits.

The British government responded to this by giving in to the demand of separate electorates for the Depressed Classes — the Communal Award of 16 August 1932. Gandhiji was very upset and began a fast unto death, and after negotiations with Ambedkar, the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, but they were to be voted in by the general electorate.

By 1930 the Muslims had become alienated from the Congress: after the decline of the Non-Cooperation–Khilafat movement a large section of Muslims felt alienated from Congress, and from the mid-1920s the Congress came to be more visibly associated with openly Hindu religious nationalist groups such as the Hindu Mahasabha. As communal riots broke out, relations between Hindus and Muslims worsened; each community organised religious processions with militant fervour, provoking Hindu–Muslim communal clashes. Muhammad Ali Jinnah was willing to give up the demand for separate electorates if Muslims were assured reserved seats in the Central Assembly and representation in proportion to population in the Muslim-dominated provinces (Bengal and Punjab) — but the Congress’s refusal to give this was a factor in the eventual division of the country.

The Sense of Collective Belonging

Nationalism spreads when people begin to believe that they are all part of the same nation, when they discover some unity that binds them together. In India, this sense of collective belonging came partly through the experience of united struggles, and partly through a variety of cultural processes through which nationalism captured people’s imagination — history and fiction, folklore and songs, popular prints and symbols, all played a part in the making of nationalism.

The identity of the nation is most often represented through images. In the twentieth century, the identity of India came to be visually associated with the image of Bharat Mata — the mother figure, first created by Abanindranath Tagore in 1905, when the Swadeshi movement was at its height. In his painting Bharat Mata is portrayed as an ascetic figure — calm, composed, divine and spiritual, holding a sheaf of paddy in one hand, a book in another, a piece of cloth in a third and a rosary in the fourth. The image was widely circulated and Deviprasad Roychowdhury composed Vande Mataram in the same period. The image was later reproduced in popular prints, and in the 1930s a poster showed Bharat Mata with a map of India and the national flag, with the slogan “The image of Bharat Mata is the image of the nation” — a visual metaphor of national unity in which the map and the flag and the mother figure were fused.

The image of Bharat Mata acquired many forms as it circulated in popular prints and was painted by different artists. Devotion to this mother figure came to be seen as evidence of one’s nationalism. It was an image that became a symbol of national identity and inspired people to fight for freedom.

Folklore and the flag

Ideas of nationalism also developed through a movement to revive Indian folklore. Nationalists believed that folklore gave a true picture of India’s authentic culture, and they collected folk tales, songs and legends — as Rabindranath Tagore himself collected ballads, hymns and rhymes, and Natesa Sastri published a massive four-volume collection of Tamil folktales, The Folklore of Southern India. For nationalists, this was a way of restoring a sense of pride in one’s past and of building a national identity out of the culture of the common people.

The swadeshi movement in Bengal, as part of the anti-Partition movement, developed the tricolour flag — the swaraj flag — as a symbol of defiance. The flag of the swaraj was designed by Gandhiji in 1921 — a tricolour (red, green and white) with a spinning wheel at the centre, symbolising the Gandhian programme of self-reliance and the dignity of labour. During the Dandi march, and in all Congress processions, the flag became an object of veneration and was carried as the symbol of the nation.

Similarly, the icon and symbol of the tricolour and the song Vande Mataram — written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in the 1870s as a hymn to the motherland and included in his novel Anandamath — became central to nationalist mobilisation. During the Swadeshi movement in Bengal, a tricolour flag (red, green and yellow) was designed and a national song was composed.

These images and symbols, and the reinterpretation of history, gave people a sense of pride in a great past: nationalists urged Indians to look into the past and discover the greatness of their own civilisation, and they wrote about the glories of India’s art and architecture, its science and literature, its mathematics and astronomy. The past was used to restore a sense of self-respect and to argue that India had once been great and could be great again.

Why Anti-Colonial Movements Are Nationalist

The growth of nationalism in the colonies is linked to an anti-colonial movement. People begin to discover their unity in the process of their struggle with colonialism: the experience of a common oppression, common laws and common humiliation creates a shared sense of being one people. In India, the anti-colonial movement provided the ground on which various groups with different grievances could come together — peasants against landlords, tribals against forest laws, workers against low wages, women against their confinement — and each of them, in the course of the struggle, learned to see their particular grievance as part of a national one.

But the unity was never complete. Each class and group felt the effects of colonialism differently, and their notions of freedom were not always the same. The Congress under Gandhiji tried to bring them together, but the differences — between peasants and landlords, between dalits and the Congress, between Hindus and Muslims, between the business class and the workers — kept surfacing. That is why the chapter ends with the limits of the movement as much as with its achievements.

How to read this timeline: the three campaigns — 1919, 1920–22 and 1930–34 — each begin with a specific law or demand (Rowlatt Act, Khilafat plus swaraj, the salt tax) and each ends with a negotiated or forced withdrawal. The pattern shows both the power and the limits of mass satyagraha.

1.

Why is the growth of nationalism in the colonies linked to an anti-colonial movement?

Model answer

Because people discover their unity in the process of struggling against colonialism. A common ruler, common laws, common economic exploitation and common humiliation create a shared sense of being one people; the anti-colonial struggle gives that sense a purpose and an organisation. In India, peasants, tribals, workers, students and women each came into the movement with their own grievance and learned to see it as part of a national one.

2.

How did the First World War help in the growth of the national movement in India?

Model answer

The war created hardship and anger: huge defence expenditure, customs duties raised, income tax introduced, prices nearly doubled between 1913 and 1918, forced recruitment in villages, and crop failures with an influenza epidemic that killed 12–13 million people. People expected these hardships to end with the war, but they did not — and the failure of the British to grant self-government after the war, together with the Rowlatt Act, turned that disappointment into a mass movement.

3.

Why were Indians outraged by the Rowlatt Act?

Model answer

Because it was passed hurriedly through the Imperial Legislative Council despite the united opposition of Indian members, and it gave the government enormous powers to repress political activity, allowing detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. It denied the basic principle that a person is presumed innocent until proved guilty, and it showed that the government would legislate over Indian objections.

4.

Why did Gandhiji decide to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement?

Model answer

Because it was turning violent — the Chauri Chaura incident of February 1922, in which a mob set fire to a police station and killed 22 policemen, convinced him that satyagrahis needed to be properly trained before they could be ready for mass struggles. He believed that a movement based on non-violence could not continue once violence had broken out.

5.

What is meant by the idea of satyagraha?

Model answer

Satyagraha is the appeal to conscience through truth and non-violence. It holds that if a cause is true and the struggle is against injustice, physical force is not necessary: a satyagrahi can win by persuading the oppressor to see the truth, without seeking vengeance or being aggressive. It requires the opponent to be willing to see the truth, and it relies on the moral power of the suffering endured by the satyagrahi.

6.

Write a newspaper report on the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

Model answer

AMRITSAR, 14 April 1919. A peaceful gathering at the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh was fired upon yesterday afternoon by troops under General Dyer, who blocked the exits and opened fire without warning. Hundreds are feared dead and many more wounded. The crowd had gathered both to protest against the Rowlatt Act and to attend the Baisakhi fair, and many villagers, unaware that martial law had been imposed, were present. General Dyer is reported to have said that his object was to “produce a moral effect”. Protests have broken out in towns across north India, and the government has responded with floggings and the bombing of villages.

7.

Write a newspaper report on the Simon Commission.

Model answer

LAHORE, February 1928. The Commission appointed to look into the working of India’s constitutional system arrived today and was met with black flags and the slogan “Go back Simon” from every party. The Commission contains not a single Indian member, and Indians of all shades of opinion have united in rejecting it. A demonstration led by Lala Lajpat Rai was lathi-charged by the police, and the veteran leader was beaten on the chest; his condition is reported to be serious.

8.

Compare the images of Bharat Mata in this chapter with the image of Germania in Chapter 1.

Model answer

Both are female allegories of the nation, but their attributes carry different messages. Germania carries a sword and wears a crown of oak leaves, with the black-red-gold flag and rays of the rising sun — she is heroic, martial and political. Abanindranath Tagore’s Bharat Mata is ascetic, calm, composed, divine and spiritual, holding a sheaf of paddy, a book, a piece of cloth and a rosary — she stands for the nation’s culture, learning, labour and spirituality rather than for war. The later 1930s poster fuses the mother figure with the map and the flag, making her territorial and political. The contrast tells us that each nationalism chose the symbols its own struggle needed.

9.

List the different social groups which joined the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1921, and explain the hopes of any three.

Model answer

Middle-class town dwellers (students, teachers, lawyers, merchants), peasants of Awadh, tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills, plantation workers of Assam, and later women, poor peasants, rich peasants and sections of the business class. Middle class: they hoped to make government schools, courts and councils unusable and thereby force the British to concede. Awadh peasants: led by Baba Ramchandra, they hoped for the abolition of begar, reduction of revenue and an end to the illegal cesses of talukdars. Plantation workers: under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859 they could not leave the tea gardens without permission; hearing of swaraj, they believed they would get land in their own villages and defied the authorities.

10.

Discuss the Salt March to make clear why it was an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism.

Model answer

Because salt was consumed by rich and poor alike and was one of the most essential items of food, the government monopoly and tax on it touched every household. Breaking the law by making salt from sea water was therefore a simple, peaceful act that anyone could repeat — and it exposed the arbitrary character of colonial law: the state was prosecuting people for picking up something from the sea. The march itself, 240 miles in 24 days with 78 volunteers, gave the movement a visible, disciplined, non-violent form that the press could follow day by day, and it drew in peasants, tribals, women and officials who resigned. It converted a demand into a national spectacle.

11.

Imagine you are a woman participating in the Civil Disobedience Movement. Explain what the experience meant to your life.

Model answer

Model answer: “I had never stepped outside my house to attend a public meeting. When Gandhiji’s call came, my husband and I went to listen to him, and then I began to attend the meetings, to spin and wear khadi, to picket liquor shops and to carry salt in processions. The police lathi-charged us and I was arrested twice. For the first time my voice was heard outside my home; the movement gave me a public life and a sense of dignity, and it taught me that the nation was something I belonged to, not something decided by men in councils.” (Student answers will vary.)

12.

Why did political leaders differ sharply over the question of separate electorates?

Model answer

Because they disagreed about what separate electorates would do. Ambedkar and dalit leaders argued that the Depressed Classes needed separate constituencies because in a general electorate dominated by upper castes their representatives would never be chosen — separate electorates were a guarantee of political voice for a socially excluded group. Gandhiji argued that separate electorates would divide Hindu society and permanently mark dalits as a separate political community, blocking their integration; he preferred reserved seats within the general electorate, and he went on a fast unto death to prevent the Communal Award. Jinnah and the Muslim League demanded separate electorates and reserved seats for Muslims, fearing that a Hindu majority would otherwise determine everything. The Poona Pact of 1932 was the compromise between the first two positions.

08

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Explain: (a) Why growth of nationalism in the colonies is linked to an anti-colonial movement. (b) How the First World War helped in the growth of the National Movement in India. (c) Why Indians were outraged by the Rowlatt Act. (d) Why Gandhiji decided to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement.

Model answer

(a) Because people discover their unity in the process of struggling against colonial rule — common oppression, laws and humiliation create a shared identity, and the anti-colonial struggle gives it organisation and purpose. (b) The war brought huge defence expenditure, doubled prices between 1913 and 1918, new taxes, forced recruitment and, with crop failures and influenza, the death of 12–13 million people; when hardship did not end with the war and self-government was not granted, anger turned into a mass movement. (c) Because the Rowlatt Act was passed over the united opposition of Indian members and allowed detention without trial for two years, denying the presumption of innocence and showing that the government would legislate regardless of Indian opinion. (d) Because the movement was turning violent — at Chauri Chaura in February 1922 a mob burnt a police station and killed 22 policemen — and he believed satyagrahis must be properly trained before mass struggle.

2.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What is meant by the idea of satyagraha?

Model answer

It is the appeal to conscience through truth and non-violence. If the cause is true and the struggle is against injustice, physical force is unnecessary: a satyagrahi wins by persuading the oppressor to see the truth rather than by forcing him, without seeking vengeance, and truth is bound to triumph ultimately.

3.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Write a newspaper report on (a) the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (b) the Simon Commission.

Model answer

(a) Amritsar, 14 April 1919: troops under General Dyer opened fire on a peaceful gathering in the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh, blocking the exits; hundreds are feared dead. The crowd had come to protest against the Rowlatt Act and to attend the Baisakhi fair, and many villagers did not know martial law had been imposed. Dyer says he wished to “produce a moral effect”. Protests have spread across north India and the government has replied with floggings and the bombing of villages. (b) Lahore, February 1928: the Simon Commission, appointed to review India’s constitutional system and containing no Indian member, was greeted with black flags and the slogan “Go back Simon” by all parties. A demonstration led by Lala Lajpat Rai was lathi-charged and the veteran leader was injured.

4.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Compare the images of Bharat Mata in this chapter with the image of Germania in Chapter 1.

Model answer

Both personify the nation as a woman, but with different attributes. Germania is martial and political — sword, oak-leaf crown, black-red-gold flag, rays of the rising sun. Bharat Mata, as painted by Abanindranath Tagore in 1905, is ascetic, calm, divine and spiritual, holding paddy, a book, cloth and a rosary; in the 1930s poster she is joined to the map of India and the national flag. The difference reflects the different tasks of the two nationalisms: one was building a state, the other was asserting a culture against colonial rule.

5.
NCERT exercise5 marks

List the different social groups which joined the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1921. Choose any three and write about their hopes and struggles.

Model answer

Middle-class town dwellers, Awadh peasants, Gudem Hills tribal peasants, Assam plantation workers, and later women, poor and rich peasants and sections of the business class. Middle class: students left schools, lawyers gave up practice and merchants refused foreign trade, hoping to make the system unworkable. Awadh peasants: under Baba Ramchandra they demanded the abolition of begar and reduction of revenue against talukdars. Plantation workers: believing swaraj would give them land in their own villages, they defied the Inland Emigration Act, left the gardens and were caught and beaten.

6.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Discuss the Salt March to make clear why it was an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism.

Model answer

Salt was used by rich and poor alike and taxed by a government monopoly, so the tax touched every household; breaking the law by making salt from sea water was a simple act anyone could repeat, and it exposed the arbitrariness of colonial law. The march of 240 miles in 24 days with 78 volunteers gave the movement a visible, disciplined form that newspapers followed daily, and it drew in peasants, tribals, women and resigning officials. It turned an abstract demand for swaraj into a concrete, repeatable act of defiance.

7.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Imagine you are a woman participating in the Civil Disobedience Movement. Explain what the experience meant to your life.

Model answer

Model answer: it gave me a public life for the first time — attending meetings, spinning and wearing khadi, picketing liquor shops, carrying salt in processions, being lathi-charged and arrested. I learned that the nation was something I belonged to and could act for, and the movement gave me a sense of dignity and of my own capacity outside the home. (Student answers will vary.)

8.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Why did political leaders differ sharply over the question of separate electorates?

Model answer

Ambedkar held that separate electorates were the only way the Depressed Classes could be sure of political voice in an electorate dominated by upper castes; Gandhiji held that they would divide Hindu society and permanently separate dalits politically, and preferred reserved seats within the general electorate, going on a fast unto death against the Communal Award; Jinnah and the Muslim League demanded separate electorates for Muslims for fear of permanent majority rule. The Poona Pact of 1932 compromised between the first two.

9.
NCERT projectProject

Find out about the anti-colonial movement in Indo-China and compare it with India’s national movement.

Model answer

In Indo-China (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia) the anti-colonial struggle against the French combined nationalism with communist organisation: the Vietminh under Ho Chi Minh fought first the French and then the Americans, and the decisive victory at Dien Bien Phu in 1954 ended French rule. Compared with India: both used mass mobilisation and both drew on a sense of cultural identity, but India’s movement was largely non-violent and constitutional under the Congress, whereas Indo-China’s was revolutionary and armed; India achieved independence in 1947 and remained one country, while Vietnam was partitioned and fought on until 1975. (Student project.)

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Explain the Rowlatt Act and the events that followed, up to Jallianwala Bagh. (5 marks)

Model answer

The Rowlatt Act of 1919 was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council despite the united opposition of Indian members. It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhiji called for a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919, with rallies, processions and strikes. The government clamped down: local leaders were picked up from Amritsar, Gandhiji was barred from Delhi, and on 10 April police fired on a peaceful procession in Amritsar, provoking attacks on banks, post offices and railway stations. Martial law was imposed under General Dyer. On 13 April 1919 a crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh — some to protest, others for the Baisakhi fair, many unaware of martial law — and Dyer blocked the exits and opened fire, killing hundreds to “produce a moral effect”. Protests spread across north India and the government replied with floggings, forced crawling and the bombing of villages.

2.

Why did Gandhiji launch the Non-Cooperation Movement? What was its programme? (5 marks)

Model answer

Because in Hind Swaraj (1909) he argued that British rule survived only through Indian cooperation, so if Indians withdrew cooperation the Raj would collapse and swaraj would come. He also wanted to unite Hindus and Muslims, and the Khilafat agitation gave him the occasion. The programme was to unfold in stages: surrender of government titles; boycott of civil services, army, police, courts and legislative councils, schools and foreign goods; and, if the government used repression, a full civil disobedience campaign. Adopted at the Nagpur session in December 1920, it began in January 1921: students left schools, lawyers gave up practice, councils were boycotted, foreign cloth was burnt and liquor shops picketed, and imports of foreign cloth fell from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore in a year.

3.

How did different social groups conceive of the idea of swaraj? (5 marks)

Model answer

Differently. The middle classes in towns saw swaraj as the end of colonial rule through the boycott of British institutions, but the boycott slowed because khadi was expensive and Indian alternatives were slow to appear. Awadh peasants under Baba Ramchandra saw it as the end of talukdars’ exactions, begar and high rents. Tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills under Alluri Sitaram Raju saw it as the restoration of their rights to the forest — grazing and fuelwood — and Raju believed India could be liberated only by force. Assam plantation workers saw swaraj as land in their own villages and the end of the Inland Emigration Act. Rich peasants wanted revenue reduced; poor peasants wanted security of tenure; the business class wanted protection from imports; women found a public role; and dalits, whom the Congress had kept at a distance, demanded separate electorates. Each group’s notion of freedom was shaped by its own experience of colonialism.

4.

Describe the Civil Disobedience Movement, including the Salt March. (5 marks)

Model answer

After the Simon Commission and the demand for Purna Swaraj at Lahore in December 1929, Gandhiji sent Viceroy Irwin eleven demands on 31 January 1930, the most important being the abolition of the salt tax, with an ultimatum to comply by 11 March. On 12 March 1930 he began the march from Sabarmati with 78 volunteers, covering about 240 miles to Dandi and reaching the coast on 6 April, where he broke the salt law by making salt from sea water. The movement spread: foreign cloth was boycotted, liquor shops picketed, peasants refused revenue and chaukidari taxes, village officials resigned and forest laws were violated. About 1,00,000 people were arrested, including Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Gandhiji; in Sholapur crowds attacked police posts and in Peshawar peaceful satyagrahis were attacked and women and children beaten. The movement was called off under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 and relaunched in 1932, ending in 1934.

5.

Explain the limits of the Civil Disobedience Movement. (5 marks)

Model answer

The movement revealed deep differences. Rich peasants (Patidars, Jats) joined against revenue demands but lost enthusiasm once these were met, since the movement did not address their other problems. Poor peasants wanted security of tenure, which the Congress did not press. The business class supported the movement but was disappointed when it was called off in 1931 and did not participate when it was relaunched. Women participated in large numbers but were not given positions of authority. The dalits were kept at a distance for fear of offending sanatanis, and Ambedkar’s demand for separate electorates produced the Communal Award and the Poona Pact. Muslims grew alienated as the Congress appeared to be associated with Hindu religious nationalist groups, and the failure to satisfy Jinnah’s demands contributed to the eventual partition.

6.

How did a sense of collective belonging develop in India? (5 marks)

Model answer

Through united struggle and through cultural processes. The image of Bharat Mata, painted by Abanindranath Tagore in 1905 as an ascetic, divine figure holding paddy, a book, cloth and a rosary, became the visual identity of the nation, reproduced in popular prints and later fused with the map and the flag. Vande Mataram, written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and included in Anandamath, became a national song during the Swadeshi movement. Folklore was revived — Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads and Natesa Sastri published The Folklore of Southern India — to restore pride in the culture of ordinary people. The swaraj flag, a tricolour with a spinning wheel designed by Gandhiji in 1921, became an object of veneration carried in processions. And history was reinterpreted to show the greatness of India’s past, giving people self-respect and the confidence that the nation could be great again.

7.

What was the Khilafat issue and how did Gandhiji use it? (3 marks)

Model answer

After the First World War and the defeat of Ottoman Turkey, rumours spread of a harsh treaty on the Ottoman emperor, the Khalifa, spiritual head of the Islamic world. A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919 under Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali to defend the Khalifa’s temporal powers. Gandhiji saw in it an opportunity to bring Muslims into a united national movement, and at the Calcutta session in September 1920 he convinced other leaders to launch non-cooperation in support of Khilafat as well as for swaraj.

8.

Explain the Poona Pact and the debate that produced it. (5 marks)

Model answer

The Congress had kept away from the dalits for fear of offending the sanatanis, and Gandhiji’s fast to change upper-caste hearts did not satisfy Dr B.R. Ambedkar, who demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes so that they could choose their own representatives. The British government conceded this in the Communal Award of 16 August 1932. Gandhiji, who believed separate electorates would permanently divide Hindu society, began a fast unto death. After negotiations, the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in the provincial and central legislative councils, but they were to be voted in by the general electorate. It was a compromise: representation was guaranteed, but within a joint electorate rather than a separate one.

9.

Why did the Simon Commission provoke protest? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because it was set up in February 1928 to look into the working of India’s constitutional system but contained not a single Indian member. All parties, from the Congress to the Muslim League, greeted it with the slogan “Go back Simon”, and when Lala Lajpat Rai led a demonstration at Lahore he was beaten by the police and died of his injuries — turning opposition into a national grievance.

10.

How did the First World War change India’s economy and politics? (3 marks)

Model answer

Economically, defence expenditure rose sharply, customs duties were raised, income tax was introduced and prices nearly doubled between 1913 and 1918, while forced recruitment and crop failures with an influenza epidemic killed 12–13 million people. Politically, people expected self-government as a reward for wartime loyalty; when it was refused and the Rowlatt Act was passed instead, the disappointment produced the first nationwide campaign under Gandhiji.

Previous year questions

CBSE pattern

Why did Gandhiji withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement? (CBSE pattern, 3 marks)

Model answer

Because it turned violent: at Chauri Chaura in February 1922 a mob set fire to a police station and killed 22 policemen. Gandhiji believed a non-violent movement could not continue after such violence, and that satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggle.

2.
CBSE pattern

Explain the significance of the Salt March. (3 marks)

Model answer

Salt was used by rich and poor alike and taxed by a government monopoly, so breaking the salt law was a simple act anyone could repeat; the 240-mile march from Sabarmati to Dandi in 24 days gave the movement a visible, disciplined, non-violent form that newspapers followed daily; and it drew in peasants, tribals, women and officials, making the Civil Disobedience Movement a mass movement.

3.
CBSE pattern

How did the image of Bharat Mata become a symbol of national identity? (3 marks)

Model answer

Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata in 1905 as an ascetic, divine figure holding paddy, a book, cloth and a rosary; the image circulated widely in popular prints and was later fused with the map of India and the national flag, with the slogan that the image of Bharat Mata is the image of the nation. Devotion to her became evidence of one’s nationalism.

4.
CBSE pattern

What was the Rowlatt Act? Why did it provoke outrage? (3 marks)

Model answer

It was an Act of 1919 allowing detention of political prisoners without trial for two years, passed despite the united opposition of Indian members. Indians were outraged because it denied the presumption of innocence and showed that the government would legislate over their objections, which led to the nationwide hartal of 6 April 1919.

5.
CBSE pattern

Why did political leaders differ over separate electorates? (3 marks)

Model answer

Ambedkar wanted separate electorates so that dalits could choose their own representatives; Gandhiji feared they would permanently divide Hindu society and preferred reserved seats in a joint electorate, fasting unto death against the Communal Award; Jinnah demanded separate electorates for Muslims. The Poona Pact of 1932 reserved seats for dalits within the general electorate.

6.
CBSE pattern

Explain the Gandhi–Irwin Pact. (2 marks)

Model answer

The agreement of 5 March 1931 under which the government agreed to release political prisoners and Gandhiji agreed to call off the Civil Disobedience Movement and attend the Second Round Table Conference in London.

7.
CBSE pattern

How did the tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills join the national movement? (3 marks)

Model answer

Under Alluri Sitaram Raju, who claimed special powers, they resented the closing of large forest areas and the ban on grazing and on collecting fuelwood and fruits. Raju was inspired by Gandhiji and persuaded people to wear khadi, but he also asserted that India could be liberated only by force.

8.
CBSE pattern

What was the Inland Emigration Act and how did it affect plantation workers? (2 marks)

Model answer

The Act of 1859 forbade plantation workers from leaving the tea gardens without permission. When they heard of the Non-Cooperation Movement and of swaraj, they believed they would get land in their own villages, defied the authorities, left the plantations and headed home — and were caught by the police and beaten.

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

What was the difference between Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience?

Model answer

Non-Cooperation (1920–22) asked Indians to withdraw cooperation from British institutions — boycott schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth. Civil Disobedience (1930–34) went further: it broke specific colonial laws openly, beginning with the salt law, and accepted the punishment.

2.

Why was salt chosen for the 1930 campaign?

Model answer

Because it was consumed by rich and poor alike, taxed under a government monopoly, and could be made by anyone from sea water — so the law could be broken by a simple, repeatable, non-violent act.

3.

Who were the sanatanis?

Model answer

Conservative high-caste Hindus, whose opposition the Congress feared when it came to raising dalit demands.

4.

What was the Communal Award?

Model answer

The British award of 16 August 1932 granting separate electorates to the Depressed Classes, which Gandhiji opposed by a fast unto death.

5.

What did the Poona Pact achieve?

Model answer

Reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in provincial and central legislative councils, elected through the general electorate — representation without a separate electorate.

6.

What was the Swaraj Party?

Model answer

A party formed within the Congress by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru to return to council politics and oppose British policies from within the legislatures.

7.

Why did the Congress not support the dalit demand at first?

Model answer

Because it feared offending the sanatanis, the conservative high-caste Hindus, which is why Ambedkar’s separate electorate demand arose outside the Congress.

8.

What was the significance of 26 January 1930?

Model answer

It was observed as Independence Day after the Lahore session of December 1929 formalised the demand for Purna Swaraj.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): The First World War helped the growth of the national movement in India.
Reason (R): It created economic hardship and raised expectations that were not fulfilled.

2.

Assertion (A): Satyagraha relies on physical force.
Reason (R): A satyagrahi appeals to the conscience of the oppressor.

3.

Assertion (A): The Rowlatt Act allowed detention without trial.
Reason (R): It was passed despite the united opposition of Indian members.

4.

Assertion (A): Jallianwala Bagh led to widespread protest in north India.
Reason (R): General Dyer fired on a peaceful gathering on 13 April 1919.

5.

Assertion (A): The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura.
Reason (R): Gandhiji felt satyagrahis needed to be properly trained.

6.

Assertion (A): Khadi was cheaper than mill-made cloth.
Reason (R): Poor people could not sustain the boycott of foreign cloth.

7.

Assertion (A): The Salt March was an effective symbol of resistance.
Reason (R): Salt was consumed by rich and poor alike.

8.

Assertion (A): The Congress fully represented the dalits in the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Reason (R): The Congress kept away from the dalits for fear of offending the sanatanis.

9.

Assertion (A): The Poona Pact provided separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
Reason (R): It gave them reserved seats voted in by the general electorate.

10.

Assertion (A): Images and symbols helped create a sense of collective belonging.
Reason (R): Bharat Mata, Vande Mataram and the swaraj flag were widely circulated.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Hind Swaraj and the logic of non-cooperation

Source extract

In his famous book Hind Swaraj (1909) Mahatma Gandhi declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians, and had survived only because of this cooperation. If Indians refused to cooperate, British rule in India would collapse within a year, and swaraj would come.

1.

What is the central argument of Hind Swaraj as summarised here?

Model answer

That colonial rule depends on the consent and cooperation of the ruled; withdraw that cooperation and the structure collapses. Swaraj is therefore not something to be begged for but something Indians can bring about by their own refusal to cooperate.

2.

How was this argument turned into a programme?

Model answer

Through the staged programme of non-cooperation: surrender of titles, boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, councils, schools and foreign goods, to be followed by full civil disobedience if the government used repression.

3.

What weakness of the argument did the movement reveal?

Model answer

That withdrawal of cooperation requires alternatives — Indian schools, courts and cloth — which were slow to appear, and that khadi was more expensive than mill cloth, so the boycott could not be sustained by the poor.

Source 2 — Jallianwala Bagh

Source extract

On 13 April 1919 a crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh. Some came to protest against the government’s new repressive measures and others to attend the annual Baisakhi fair. Being from outside the city, many villagers were unaware of the martial law that had been imposed. Dyer entered the area, blocked the exit points, and opened fire on the crowd, killing hundreds. His object, as he declared later, was to “produce a moral effect”, to create in the minds of satyagrahis a feeling of terror and awe.

1.

Why were so many ordinary villagers present?

Model answer

Because it was Baisakhi, and many had come from outside the city for the fair; being from outside, they did not know that martial law had been imposed.

2.

What did Dyer intend, and what did he achieve?

Model answer

He intended a “moral effect” — terror and awe among satyagrahis. What he achieved was the opposite: the massacre outraged India, protests spread across north India, and it became one of the founding grievances of the mass national movement.

3.

What does the episode show about colonial rule?

Model answer

That it rested ultimately on coercion, and that it would use overwhelming force against unarmed people. The crawling order and the bombing of villages that followed showed the same logic.

Source 3 — Why salt?

Source extract

Gandhiji found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation. On 31 January 1930 he sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands. Some of these were of general interest; others were specific demands of different classes, from industrialists to peasants. The idea was to make the demands wide-ranging, so that all classes within Indian society could identify with them and everyone could be brought together in a united campaign. The most stirring of all was the demand to abolish the salt tax. Salt was something consumed by the rich and the poor alike, and it was one of the most essential items of food. The tax on salt and the government monopoly over its production, Mahatma Gandhi declared, revealed the most oppressive face of British rule.

1.

Why was the demand for abolishing the salt tax chosen as the central one?

Model answer

Because salt was consumed by rich and poor alike and was an essential item of food; the tax and the monopoly therefore affected every household, and Gandhiji could say they revealed the most oppressive face of British rule.

2.

Why were eleven demands sent rather than one?

Model answer

To make the demands wide-ranging so that all classes — industrialists, peasants and others — could identify with the campaign and be brought together in a united movement.

3.

What does this tell us about how Gandhiji built a mass movement?

Model answer

That he chose issues which were both universal in their reach and concrete in their effect, and that he deliberately connected the specific grievances of different classes to a single national demand.

Map-Based Practice

Locate and label on the outline map

How to practise

Read the task, then say or write the location before revealing the answer. Where a textbook map is available it is shown above with hotspots you can tap.

Map work — the geography of the movement

The map above is the original NCERT map — tap it to zoom. Then tap a numbered label below to check what to locate and where it lies.

1.

On an outline map of India, mark the places associated with Gandhiji’s early satyagrahas and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

Model answer

Champaran in Bihar (1916), Kheda in Gujarat (1917), Ahmedabad in Gujarat (1918) and Amritsar in Punjab (13 April 1919).

2.

Trace the route of the Salt March on a map and mark the distance.

Model answer

From Sabarmati Ashram near Ahmedabad, through Aslali, Nadiad, Anand, Borsad, Bhadran and Borsad-side villages to Dandi on the coast — about 240 miles (385 km), covered in 24 days from 12 March to 6 April 1930.

3.

Mark the areas of peasant and tribal movements during Non-Cooperation.

Model answer

Awadh in Uttar Pradesh (Baba Ramchandra), the Gudem Hills in Andhra Pradesh (Alluri Sitaram Raju), and the tea plantations of Assam.

4.

Locate the places of confrontation during the Civil Disobedience Movement: Peshawar, Sholapur and Dharasana.

Model answer

Peshawar in the North-West Frontier Province, where peaceful satyagrahis were attacked; Sholapur in Maharashtra, where crowds attacked police posts, municipal buildings, law courts and railway stations; and Dharasana in Gujarat, where salt depots were raided.

17

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

Why did the same movement attract rich peasants, poor peasants and the business class, and why did each leave it?

Model answer

Because each joined for its own reason. Rich peasants joined against revenue demands and left once the government conceded; poor peasants wanted security of tenure, which the Congress never pressed; the business class wanted protection from imports and a favourable exchange rate, was disappointed when the movement was called off in 1931 and stayed away when it was relaunched. A mass movement can be broad only by holding different grievances together, and it weakens when any group’s specific demand is settled. (Model answer.)

2.

“Gandhiji’s fast unto death was a political weapon, not a religious act.” Discuss.

Model answer

It was both, and that is why it worked. It was religious in form — self-suffering rather than coercion, appealing to the conscience — and political in effect: it forced a negotiation with Ambedkar and produced the Poona Pact within weeks, preventing the separate electorates that Gandhiji believed would divide Hindu society. Its power came precisely from the fact that it was not a threat to others but a threat to himself, which placed the moral cost of refusal on his opponents. (Model answer.)

3.

Would the Non-Cooperation Movement have succeeded if Chauri Chaura had not happened?

Model answer

Probably not in the short run. The movement was already slowing in the cities because khadi was costly and Indian alternatives to British schools and courts were slow to appear; the government had not collapsed as Hind Swaraj predicted. Chauri Chaura gave Gandhiji the occasion to withdraw, but the deeper reasons were the movement’s limited capacity to replace the institutions it boycotted. Its real achievement was to make the Congress a mass organisation and to create a vocabulary of non-violent protest that would be used for decades. (Model answer.)

4.

How did the failure to accommodate dalit and Muslim demands shape the future of Indian nationalism?

Model answer

It narrowed the Congress’s claim to represent all Indians. The dalit question produced the Communal Award and the Poona Pact, and left a separate political identity for the Depressed Classes; the Muslim question, after the decline of Khilafat, the Congress’s association with Hindu Mahasabha-type groups and the refusal to concede reserved seats in proportion to population, fed the demand for Pakistan. The chapter is careful to present these as processes rather than single decisions — but the direction is clear: a movement that could not hold its minorities together would eventually be partitioned. (Model answer.)

5.

Why was Bharat Mata shown as an ascetic rather than a warrior, unlike Germania?

Model answer

Because the two nationalisms were doing different work. Germania was mobilising a people to found a state through war, so she carries a sword and wears oak leaves. Abanindranath Tagore’s Bharat Mata, painted in 1905 at the height of Swadeshi, was asserting a civilisation against a colonial claim of superiority: she holds paddy, a book, cloth and a rosary — the nation’s labour, learning, industry and spirituality — and her calm divinity was a rebuke to the idea that India was merely a subject territory. Later, in the 1930s, she was given the map and the flag, becoming territorial and political as the movement became a demand for statehood. (Model answer.)

6.

A student says: “The Congress was a Hindu party.” Evaluate.

Model answer

Too simple. The Congress was a broad coalition — its 1920 programme was adopted with Khilafat leaders, its cadres included Muslims, and Gandhiji worked hard for Hindu–Muslim unity. But the charge has a basis in the 1920s and 1930s: the Congress kept away from dalit demands for fear of offending sanatanis, and after the Khilafat movement declined it came to be associated with openly Hindu religious nationalist groups, while refusing Jinnah’s conditions for Muslim representation. So it was not a Hindu party, but it failed to convince many Muslims that it was not — and that failure had consequences. (Model answer.)

One page before the exam

War and aftermath

  • 1914–18: defence expenditure, taxes, prices doubled 1913–18, forced recruitment.
  • 1918–21 crop failure, influenza — 12–13 million dead (1921 Census).
  • Expectations of self-government disappointed.

Satyagraha

  • Appeal to conscience through truth and non-violence.
  • Champaran 1916, Kheda 1917, Ahmedabad 1918.

1919

  • Rowlatt Act — detention without trial.
  • 6 April hartal; 13 April Jallianwala Bagh; crawling order; Gandhiji calls off.

Non-Cooperation

  • Hind Swaraj 1909: British rule rests on Indian cooperation.
  • Khilafat Committee March 1919; Calcutta Sept 1920; Nagpur Dec 1920 adopts programme.
  • Begins January 1921; foreign cloth imports Rs 102 cr → Rs 57 cr.
  • Awadh (Baba Ramchandra), Gudem Hills (Raju), Assam plantations.
  • Chauri Chaura Feb 1922 — 22 policemen killed; movement withdrawn; Swaraj Party formed.

Civil Disobedience

  • Simon Commission 1928; Lahore Dec 1929 — Purna Swaraj; 26 Jan 1930.
  • Salt March 12 March–6 April 1930; 240 miles; about 1,00,000 arrested.
  • Gandhi–Irwin Pact 5 March 1931; Second Round Table Conference; relaunched 1932; ends 1934.
  • Limits: rich and poor peasants, business class, women, dalits, Muslims.

Dalits and Muslims

  • Ambedkar demands separate electorates; Communal Award 16 Aug 1932; fast; Poona Pact Sept 1932.
  • Muslim alienation after Khilafat; Jinnah’s demands refused; road to partition.

Collective belonging

  • Bharat Mata — Abanindranath Tagore, 1905; ascetic figure.
  • Vande Mataram — Bankim Chandra, Anandamath.
  • Folklore — Tagore, Natesa Sastri; swaraj flag with spinning wheel, 1921.
  • Reinterpretation of history for self-respect.

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

The First World War created a new economic and political situation in India — huge defence expenditure, new taxes, prices that nearly doubled between 1913 and 1918, forced recruitment, and crop failures with an influenza epidemic that killed 12 to 13 million people. When the expected reward of self-government did not come, anger found a leader and a method. Gandhiji returned in January 1915 and used satyagraha — the appeal to conscience through truth and non-violence — at Champaran in 1916, Kheda in 1917 and Ahmedabad in 1918. The Rowlatt Act of 1919, allowing detention without trial, produced a nationwide hartal, and on 13 April 1919 General Dyer fired on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds to “produce a moral effect”. The repression that followed — forced crawling, floggings, the bombing of villages — turned nationalism into a mass movement.

The Non-Cooperation Movement, adopted at Nagpur in December 1920 and launched in January 1921, combined the Khilafat issue with swaraj and asked Indians to withdraw cooperation from British institutions: titles, schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth. Students left schools, lawyers gave up practice, foreign cloth imports fell from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore. But the movement slowed because khadi was expensive and Indian alternatives were slow to appear, and it was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura in February 1922. Within it, peasants of Awadh under Baba Ramchandra, tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills under Alluri Sitaram Raju and plantation workers of Assam each pursued their own notion of swaraj.

After the Simon Commission of 1928 and the Lahore demand for Purna Swaraj in 1929, the Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Salt March from Sabarmati to Dandi, 12 March to 6 April 1930, and about 1,00,000 people were arrested. It ended with the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 1931, was relaunched in 1932 and closed in 1934. Its limits were exposed by the different demands of rich and poor peasants, the business class, women, dalits and Muslims: the Communal Award and the Poona Pact settled the dalit question only by compromise, and the Congress’s failure to satisfy Muslim demands contributed to partition.

A sense of collective belonging was built through struggle and through culture — Abanindranath Tagore’s Bharat Mata, Bankim Chandra’s Vande Mataram, revived folklore, the swaraj flag with its spinning wheel, and a reinterpretation of history that restored pride in India’s past. Nationalism in the colonies grew out of anti-colonial struggle; but its unity was always incomplete, and its history is a record of what a mass movement could achieve and what it could not hold together.
